OURNAL OF GEOPHYSICAL RESEARCH VOL. 73, NO. 2 JANUARY 15, 1968 Paleomagnetism of Kamthi Sandstones of Upper Permian Age from Godavary Valley, India 1. K. VERMA AND M. S. B HALLA National Geophysical Research Institute, Hyderabad, India The palcomagnetism of fifty-seven rock samples of red sandstones, collected from three sites, belonging to the Kamthi formation of Upper Permian age has been studied. The natural remanent magnetization of most of the samples showed normal polarization with upward dip (declination close to 360 ø defined as normal). The intensity of magnetization of the samples ranged from I to 10 X 10 -6 gauss. The samples were demagnetized in peak alternating fields of 50, 100, 200, 400, and 600 oersteds. The grouping of the vectors improved considerably on demagnetization. Mean direction for the three sites after ac cleaning was 306øE and --50 ø (up) after applying dip correction. The corresponding virtual geomagnetic pole is situated at 18øN, 53øW. The results are consistent with India's being in the southern hemisphere during Upper Permian times, when it might have been a part of Gondwanaland along with the Con- tinents of Africa, Australia, Antarctica, and South America. Introduction. The palcomagnet

traps (Upper Cretaceous to Mio- cene) and of the Raimahal and Sylhet traps (probably Jurassic) provide evidence for the drift of the Indian land mass from southern latitudes since the Jurassic to its present posi- tion in the northern hemisphere [Clegg et al., 1956, 1958; Deutsch et al., 1958, 1959; Atha- vale et al., 1963]. There is a wide gap from Jurassic to Precambrian in the study of paleo- magneteism of Indian rocks. As continental drift is a major phenomenon, which appears to have occurred from the Carboniferous to Tertiary, it is important to study rock forma- tions spanning this entire period of time. Fine-grained red sandstones and shales have been found to be particularly suitable for palco- magnetic studies, as they have very often yielded stable directions of magnetization. Red- beds of Permian and Triassic age have been studied in other fragments of Gondwanaland. Results from Africa lOpdyke, 1964], South America [Creer, 1965], and Australia [Irving, 1963] are available. In this paper, results from fine-grained red sandstones of the Kamthi for- mation of Upper Permian age from Godavary Valley are reported. Geology and sampling. The Wardha-Goda- vary valley is a well-known Gondwana trough in southern India, which runs in a general NW- SE direction from near Rajahmundry (17øN, 81ø48'E) to near Chanda (20øN, 79ø2YE). The valley is 50-65 km wide and is flanked on either side by Precambrian metamorphic rocks. It is filled with sediments ranging in age from Carboniferous to Cretaceous. The Kamthi for- marion is exposed over a distance of nearly 320 km along the western margin of the valley. The stratigraphic sequence [King, 1880.; Krishnan, 1960] is given in Table 1. The general strike of the formations is NW- SE, and the dip is about 10 ø to NE. The tectonic evidence sug- gests that the intrusion of the Ntonya ring structure an'd other similar complexes was as- sociated with this last major phase of activity [Bloomfield, 1965]. The structure is, therefore, regarded as having a minimum age of 520 m.y., and the most probable age is about 600 m.y. The time of cooling through the Curie point is likely to have been closer to the time of intru- sion than to the time recorded by the K/Ar ages. Unfortunately, the presence of a large IRM component prevents the detection of a viscous PTRM [Chamalaun, 1964; Briden, 1965], which would be expected if the rocks were maintained for tens of millions of years at elevated temperatures below the Curie point. The palcomagnetism and age determil{ations rule out a metamorphic event at temperatures approaching the Curie point. Beyond this they do not help to discriminaie between the view of Clifford [1967] that there was a major tectono-thermal event at about 500 m.y. an'd that of Cahen and Snelling [1966] that, if there was any event at that time (which they doubt), it was 'essentially mild' 'though pos- sibly pervasive.' The mean direction of stable NRM was 311.3øE, +42.8 ø (downward), which corresponds on the geocentric dipole model to a palcomagnetic pole at 15.1øN, 27.8øW. MCELHINNY 2 Physics Department, University College o Rhodesia Salisbury, Rhodesia Samples have been collected from twelve sites at four different localities through the Waterberg red bed succession in the Transvaal. The samples respond equally well to both thermal and magnetic cleaning, and in most cases there is no significant difference between the results obtained by the two methods. After magnetic cleaning at all the sites and cor- recting for the attitude of the beds in each case, the directions of magnetization form three groups. These groups appear to be related to the stratigraphic position of the sites in the succession. It is suggested that these changes in direction of magnetization through the sequence are the result of considerable polar wandering which took place during the period of deposition and consolidation of the Waterberg sediments. A pure-shear deforma- tion of such a zone by a stress directed from SE to NW can be expected to form primary tension fractures trending mostly NW-SE. If simple-shear deformation took place in a zone trending NE-SW, tension fractures can be ex- pected to cut that zone diagonally. These frac- tures originate at an angle of about 45 ø to the main shear plane (here supposedly trending more or less NE-SW); they will rotate syn- chronously with the polarity of the movements. 'OURNAL OF GEOPHYSICAL RESEARCH VOL. 72, No. 8 APRIL 15, 1957 Paleomagnetic-Tectonic Study of Mesozoic Dike Swarms in the Appalachians JELLE DE BOER Wesleyan University, Middletown, Connecticut Palcomagnetic evidence indicates that most of the extensive dike swarms cutting Triassic and older formations probably intruded in a time of regional tectonic and magmatic activity distinct from the late Triassic tectogenesis. The fossil magnetic directions of the dikes coin- cide neither with Late Triassic nor with Early Cretaceous palcomagnetic directions, which suggests a Jurassic age for the intrusions. The dikes were emplaced along tensional fractures that were the surficial expressions of deep-seated movements. The fan-shaped arrangement of these fractures indicates a southwestward decrease of the rotational component of the shear couple and a sinistral polarity of the shear movements. Periodic increases in tectonic and mafic magmatic activity, such as this one in the Jurassic, appear to be characteristic of Mesozoic deformations in the Appalachians. SUMMARY AND DISCUSSION The major part of the NRM in rock units investigated is primary, although secondary magnetic components have been added to out- crops of many rock units. Most of the secondary magnetization is believed to be iso- thermal reinanent magnetization (IRM) pro- duced by lightning; some secondary magneti- zation may be VRM acquired in the earth's field. Lightning-induced magnetization has been recognized by the localized occurrence of anomalous magnetization in isolated outcrops, by the general character of the outcrop terrain which in places includes lightning-struck nat- ural objects such as trees, and by the typical hardness of the magnetization which may ordi- narily be randomized in peak alternating fields of less than 450 oe. NRM directions of most rock units are grouped in either a normal or reversed sense after partial demagneti- zation, although directions of a few units of probable mudflow origin are highly dispersed. No evidence of self-reversed magnetization has been found; consequently, a field polarity sequence has been tentatively established in connection with Late Cretaceous and early Tertiary orogenic events. All folded rocks investigated belong to the Upper Cretaceous Elk- horn Mountains Volcanics; stratigraphic correlation between widely separated, structurally dissimilar outcrops of petrologically similar rocks is supported by NRM directions and polarities. Mean NRM directions of structurally restored, age-equivalent sites do not differ significantly from one another, which suggests that fold axes are nearly horizontal; however, they differ significantly from directions of nearby fiat-lying volcanic rocks of probable Tertiary

SUMMARY AND DISCUSSION The major part of the NRM in rock units investigated is primary, although secondary magnetic components have been added to out- crops of many rock units. Most of the secondary magnetization is believed to be iso- thermal reinanent magnetization (IRM) pro- duced by lightning; some secondary magneti- zation may be VRM acquired in the earth's field. Lightning-induced magnetization has been recognized by the localized occurrence of anomalous magnetization in isolated outcrops, by the general character of the outcrop terrain which in places includes lightning-struck nat- ural objects such as trees, and by the typical hardness of the magnetization which may ordi- narily be randomized in peak alternating fields of less than 450 oe. The deviation of the declination of the paleomagnetic directions in northeast Italy, Corsica, and northeast Spain are indicative of counterclockwise rotations. These rotations are thought to be related to the dextral shear movements mentioned above. They were caused by subsidiary left lateral shear which developed in the mobile zones bordering the primary dextral faults. Similar structural systems are found in the former Tethys areas of Turkey (Anatolia fault system) and northwest Africa (Atlas fault system). The main conclusion drawn from the paleomagnetic data is that the Tethys mobile belt was and still is a zone of primary dextral shear. Introduction. The deviation of the declination of the paleomagnetic directions in northeast Italy, Corsica, and northeast Spain are indicative of counterclockwise rotations. These rotations are thought to be related to the dextral shear movements mentioned above. They were caused by subsidiary left lateral shear which developed in the mobile zones bordering the primary dextral faults. Similar structural systems are found in the former Tethys areas of Turkey (Anatolia fault system) and northwest Africa (Atlas fault system). The only known occurrence of igneous ro cks within these beds is that at the eastern tip of George Island (p a rt of Hog Island), Malpequ e Bay. These ro cks appear to have been injected as a sill into the red sandstones while the latter were still undistu rbed and apparently unconsolidated. The age of the islands is rather uncertain; the oldest rocks are pre- Miocene, probably Oligocene, and the major intrusions are attributed to the Upper and Middle Miocene. The majority of the islands are composed of tuffs and lavas ranging in age from about mid-Pliocene to the present; active volcanoes being on Ambrym, Lopevi, Tanna and in the Banks Islands and off the island of Epi. Twelve sites were visited on six islands (Fig. 1); 37 hand samples were collected from natural exposures, mostly along the sea coasts. These sam- ples were drilled in the laboratory and the natural remanent magnetization (N.M.R.) of 75 specimens was measured, using astatic magnetometers (Blackett, 1952; Collinson et al., 1957), with an accuracy of 3” in direction and 5% in intensity. The exact age of the samples is not known although samples from Ambrym were thought to be from a lava and associated tuff erupted in 1913, and samples from Lopevi are almost certainly of historic age. PALAEOMAGNETIC OBSERVATIONS Sixteen samples were collected at two sites about 2-3 km apart on either side of the village of Ota. At both sites fresh surfaces were exposed in road cuttings and sampling was spread over a lateral distance of at least 100 m of outcrop in each case. These outcrops were not unbroken, and in TELLINGEN'S (1955) sense would represent several enclaves. From each hand sample a single 2.5 cm core was prepar- ed on which measurements of direction and intensity of magnetization and alternating field demagnetization tests were carried out. Only two specimens proved to be insufficiently magnetic to give results under the short period low sensitivity astatic magnetometer used. Progressive demagnetization was carried out in fields of up to about 700 Oe with little change in direction. The best re- presentation of the recorded direction of magnetization was regarded as that in which the mean value was associated with the maximum value of k (FISHER, 1953). ow widely accept the idea that the geomagnetic field has reversed itself in the geological past. This hypothesis has become more and more con- vincing as additional paleomagnetic and rock magnetic data have accumulated. However, there still remains the possibility of naturally occurring self-reversal of the magnetic polarity in some rocks. Very few cases have been reported in which the self-reversing properties of rock-forming ferrimagnetic minerals could be demonstrated in the laboratory (Uyeda, 1958; Carmichael, 1959; Havard and Lewis, 1965), but some of the self-reversal mechanisms may not be reproducible on a laboratory time scale (Neel, 1951; Verhoogen, 1956). Ade-Hall (1964) reported a fairly strong correlation between the polarity of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) and the stage of alteration or oxidation of minerals in basalt lavas of Mull, Scotland. Although paleomagnetic studies did not reveal systematic differ- ences between normal and reversed lava flows (Wilson, 1964), Ade-Hall claimed on the basis of his petrological observations that a self-reversal mechanism might be responsible for the NRM of the reversed flows. The results of these studies have strongly supported the continental drift theory of the Indian land- mass between Jurassic to Miocene times from the southern hemisphere to its present position in the northern hemisphere. Hargraves (1959) obtained a field vector for the Lac Tio ilmenite deposit, but not knowing whether the Lac Tio deposit had remained undisturbed since its magnetization, he did not attempt the calculation of a "pole position". The directions of natural remanent magnetism (n.r.m.) of other rock samples col- lected throughout the Allard Lake area were widely scattered, and for lack of facilities for magnetic cleaning in 1959, the paleomagnetic study was not concluded. The anor- thosite mountain is then regarded as part of the area of central uplift com- parable with other supposed meteorite craters on the earth, the moon, and Mars, and the dacitic material is the product of shock melting and ejection from the region of impact (Dence 1965). GEOLOGY AND SAMPLING The circular feature is set in an area of Precambrian foliated gneisses, basic intrusive rocks, and metasediments of the Grenville (structural) Province. Most of the area within the twin lakes is covered by the dacitic material, which is in places more than 700 ft thick, and lies nearly horizontally on the basement. Mount de Babel, the prominent anorthositic central feature, rises to an eleva- tion of more than 3000 ft. The dacite may be divided into a lower fine-grained and commonly inclusion-rich part, and an upper coarser-grained part in which inclusions are not so common. Some years ago similar investigations in the Spanish Pyrenees by VAN DER LINGEN (1960) and SCHWARZ (1962, 1963) yielded virtual Permo-Triassic pole positions that were different from those for stable (extra alpine) Europe. Their results indicated a counterclockwise rotation of Spain (GIRDLER, 1965), postulated previously by several authors (DE TOIT, 1937; CAREV, 1958; BULLARD et al., 1965). Recent investigations (VAN DER VOO, 1967, and the present paper) on volcanic and sedimentary rocks lead to firmer based palaeomagnetic evidence for the rotation of the Iberian peninsula. VAN DER VOO Palaeomagnetie Laboratory Fort HoofddUk, State University, Utrecht (The Netherlands) (Received February 2, 1967) SUMMARY The magnetic properties of 39 oriented samples of Triassic siltstones and of 43 oriented samples of Silurian andesites and basalts from the Spanish Meseta were investigated. After a.c. magnetic field demagnetization up to 3,000 Oe, peak value, and after correction for the dip of the geological strata the Triassic samples revealed a characteristic direction of magnetization with an average declination (D) of 359.5 ° and an inclination (I) of 23 °. One group of samples of Silurian volcanic rocks from tile province of Guadalajara had, after a.c. magnetic field demagneti- zation and correction for the dip, a characteristic direction of magnetization with an average declination of 159 ° and an inclination of 18.5°; another group from the province of Ciudad Real had, after a.c. magnetic field demagnetization and after correction for the dip, a characteristic direction of magnetization with an average declination of 130.5 ° and an inclination of 22.5 ° .

ian volcanic rocks from tile province of Guadalajara had, after a.c. magnetic field demagneti- zation and correction for the dip, a characteristic direction of magnetization with an average declination of 159 ° and an inclination of 18.5°; another group from the province of Ciudad Real had, after a.c. magnetic field demagnetization and after correction for the dip, a characteristic direction of magnetization with an average declination of 130.5 ° and an inclination of 22.5 ° . The palaeomagnetic pole position derived from the Triassic rocks is situated at 63°N 177.5°E, and the pole positions of the first and second group of Silurian samples are situated at 35.5°N 157°W and 21°N 132°W, respectively. The divergency between these results and the already known data for Trias- sic and Silurian from stable (extra-Alpine) Europe highly supports a counter- clockwise rotation of Spain. section_candidates.excerpt: ighbourhood of Almad6n, where five samples have been collected from one flow of the basaltic rocks intercalated between Silurian quartzites and fossiliferous shales. Five more samples have been taken from one dacitic flow near the railway station of Almadenejos, situated at 11.5 km east of Almad6n. METHODS OF RESEARCH The samples were sawn to approximately equidimensional shape and embed- ded in their correct orientation in cubes of paraffin with 10-cm edges; thereupon directions and intensities were measured on the Utrecht astatic magnetometers. The natural remanent magnetization (N.R.M.) of all samples was analysed by progressive demagnetization with a.c. magnetic fields up to 3,000 Oe (peak value). For an extensive description of the methods of measurement and the analysis of the N.R.M. with the aid of a.c. magnetic field demagnetization the reader is referred to As and ZIJDERVELD (1958), AS (1960), and ZIJDERVELD (1967a). The numerical data thus obtained are summarized in Table I and II, and Fig.3, 5 and 7 show the data plotted in stereographic projection. The correction for the geomagnetic variation has been applied. RESULTS OF THE TRIASSIC SAMPLES (SAMPLES VAL 1-34, ALC 1-3, ALC 21-23) The intensity of the N.R.M. of the siltstones varied between21.10 -6 and 4.10 -6 e.m.

These magnetic properties suggest that the remanence of the upper slate member is composed of two or more components. Probably, the primary d.r.m. or c.r.m. of the upper slates has been mostly obliterated by contact metamorphism during intrusion of the Nipissing sill, which impressed a secondary remanence on the slates. This secondary remanence is probably a t.r.m. associated with heating to a temperature of about 500 f 75 "C, which is the probable Curie Point range for the primary ferromagnetic minerals, or possibly a c.r.m. associated with hydrothermal chemical reactions. Detailed minerdogic studies of the ferromagnetic minerals should distinguish between the t.r.m. and c.r.rn. alterna- tives. It does suggest that a 500 & 75 "C contact metamorphic isotherm could be drawn at or near the base of the upper slate or 20 to 25 ft below the Nipissing sill. Barker (1966) placed a 300 OC isotherm at about the same distance on petrologic evidence. CONCLUSIONS 1. Palaeomagnetic results from the Hawaiian Islands have been described earlier (Doell & Cox 1961,1963, Tarling 1965) and the presence of reversals of magnetization in Samoa has been noted previously (Tarling 1962). The Samoan and Tongan Islands are in close proximity but these islands are representative of two distinct geological environments. Introduction The Hawaiian Archipelago consists of a chain of volcanic islands, reefs and shoals stretching some 2 600 km along a north-west-south-east arc. The main islands (Figure l), which lie at the south-eastern end of the arc, are composed mainly of rapidly erupted “primitive:’ olivine-basalt lavas dipping at angles between 5” and 20” and often veneered with later, more acidic lava. The age of these islands was thought, on the grounds of morphology, raised beaches, dissection, etc., to decrease in general from north-west to south-east and to range from Recent to early or middle Tertiary (Stearns 1946). Recent radioactive dating and palaeomagnetic work (Tarling 1962; McDougall & Tarling 1963, 1964; McDougall 1963, 1964) have confirmed this general trend in age but have shown the rocks to be younger than previously thought and the samples vary in age from just over 5 million years (m.y.) to less than 1 m.y. Measurements of the magnetic susceptibility and the intensity and direction of remanent magnetization were made on 325 2.5-cm cylindrical cores prepared from 189 samples of the felsites, granites, and diabases exposed in the Ironton, Fredericktown, and Coldwater quadrangles, Missouri. These measurements show, first, that the directions of remanent mag- netization, although quite variable, are significantly different from the direction of the present geomagnetic field in southeast Missouri and, second, that partial demagnetization in an ac field of 300 to 700 oe greatly improves the initial scatter of the remanent magnetization vector by diminishing the anomalous components of viscous and isothermal remanent mag- netization shown by many samples. The paleomagnetic data from five rock units indicate a Precambrian geomagnetic pole in the vicinity of 150øW and 5øN. Introduction. The St. Francois Mountains of southeast Missouri encompass about 2500 mi  in Iron, Madison, and St. Francois Counties (see Figure 1). These mountains, which are char- acterized by rolling, knob-like hills of Pre- cambrian igneous rocks, stand some 500 to 1700 feet in relief above the surrounding terrain. The igneous rocks of this area have been ex- tensively investigated petrologically by Tolman and Robertson [1960] and others. The present work represents the first extensive effort to in- vestigate the paleomagnetic properties of these relatively undisturbed Precambrian rocks. Geology and sampling. The Precambrian igneous rocks of the St. Francois Mountains fall into three major petrologic groups: a variegated series of granites, a system of basic intrusives of gabbroic composition, and a group of intrusive and extrusive felsites of rhyolitic composition. Par- tial demagnetization in alternating fields may be used to obtain information of two types in paleomagnetic research. The technique may first be used as an analytical tool to determine whether two or more components of magnetiza- tion with different degrees of magnetic hardness are present in the NRM. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: Doell and Cox, 1963]. ?ALEOMAGNETIC ACCURACY The problem of paleomagnetic accuracy we take as the problem of determining how closely the average direction of remanent magnetization of a set of lava flows corresponds to the regional geomagnetic field direction at the time each flow cooled. In our earlier study of historic Hawaiian lava flows we showed that an accuracy of 3 ø to 5 ø was possible if five to eight samples were collected from each flow. Om)¾xE  Physics Department University College o/Rhodesia and Nyasaland Salisbury, Southern Rhodesia Abstract. Samples have been collected from twelve sites in red horizons of lower Permian (Ecca) age in southwest Tanganyika. Two directions of magnetization are observed, one steeply inclined with north-seeking poles down and the other with south-seeking poles down in the direction of the earth's present magnetic field. Specimens from all the sites were sub- jected to both alternating-field and thermal demagnetization. These laboratory studies show that the component which is north-seeking down with steep inclination is the stable direction of magnetization. It is suggested that the component aligned along the earth's present field is due to the growth of hematite (CRM) in this field. After treatment at temperatures of 300øC, specimens from nine of the twelve sites gave well-grouped directions of magnetization. On the assumption of a geocentric axial dipole field, the mean pole position is at 38.2øS, 64.9øE (A95 = 16ø). This pole position places southern and eastern Africa in temperate or cold- temperate climatic zones, which is in accord with the available paleoclimati½ evidence. The polarity (reversed) of the Ecca of southwest Tanganyika is in accord with all other Permian rocks that have previously been studied. Introduction. It is most probable that the magnetiza- tion of all sites occurred in the Permian, and most likely in the lower Permian; however an upper Permian age for the Galula sites cannot be ruled out at the present time. The polarity of the sites is in accord with all other Permian results available in the literature with the single exceptions of the Upper Tartarian of Russia [Irving and Parry, 1963]. The paleoclimatic implications o/ the Permian pole position /rom A/rica. It has long been maintained by southern hemisphere geologists that during the Ecca stage of the Karroo sys- tem southern Africa lay in high latitudes. The reason for this contention is that the Ecca is the rock unit which is deposited on the glacial tillires, varves, and glacial pavements of the Dwyka glacial horizon. The reality and inten- sity of the Dwyka glaciation in Africa has sel- dom been questioned and is well documented [du Toit, 1954; Flint, 1961]. The Dwyka gla- ciation is remarkably extensive, and glacial tills and varvites have been recorded from the Congo, Southern Rhodesia, Northern Rhodesia, Tanganyika, and South-West Africa, as well as from the well-known localities of the Republic of South Africa. Samples have been collected from twelve sites in red horizons of lower Permian (Ecca) age in southwest Tanganyika. Two directions of magnetization are observed, one steeply inclined with north-seeking poles down and the other with south-seeking poles down in the direction of the earth's present magnetic field. This pole position places southern and eastern Africa in temperate or cold- temperate climatic zones, which is in accord with the available paleoclimati½ evidence. The polarity (reversed) of the Ecca of southwest Tanganyika is in accord with all other Permian rocks that have previously been studied. Introduction. The Red Sandstone formation [Gait, 1959] consists predominantly of fine-grained, well-stratified, mostly arkosic, red-colored sand- stones. Limy sandstones and impure limestones are also present. This formation conformably overlies the Sandstone and Interbedded Mud- stone formation. The boundary between the two is arbitrary. The relationship of the Red Sandstone formation with the overlying Batoka basalts is not clear, but an unconformity may be present.

Red beds have been exten- sively used in paleomagnetic research. However, the age of their natural remanent magnetiza- tion (NRM) is often unknown because it is possible that this might be a chemical remanent magnetization and therefore younger than the geological age of the rocks. This is in contrast with igneous rocks which usually acquire their magnetization on cooling through the Curie point of the magnetic minerals contained in them. Two methods exist for testing the age of the NRM of sedimentary rocks. One is based on field tests, such as the fold test and conglomerate test [Graham, 1949], and the other is based on the comparison between igneous rocks and sedimentary rocks of the same age. In this re- spect the Devonian of Great Britain poses sev- eral problems. world's rocks are magnetized normally, that is, in directions consistent with the earth's dipole moment in its present sense, and that the other 50% are reversely magnetized, in directions consistent with a reversed dipole moment of the earth~ There are apparently only two possible explanations of the reversed magnetizations, namely either (i) that for approximately 50% of geological time the earth's dipole moment has actually been reversed (field reversal), or (if) that the reversely magnetized specimens pos- sess, or have possessed, some intrinsic proper- ty which has either enabled them to become magnetized in directions opposite to those of the ambient fields in which they were laid down, or has enabled normal magnetizations to reverse at some time subsequent to their acquisition (self- reversal) [1, 2], The evidence for and against field reversal and self-reversal has been reviewed by Wil- son [3, 4]° In favour of the predominance of field reversal is the evidence from baked con- tacts [3-5], reversals "caught in the act" [6-13] and the dating of polarity epochs [9, 14-23]. [24-30] suggest the possibility of self-reversal.
